summary: Requires DNS software that claims support for DNSSEC or A6 records to also support EDNS0. These features make messages larger, and without EDNS0 queries fall back to TCP, hurting latency and server load. It updates RFC 2535.

plainLanguage.summary: DNS replies that include signatures or IPv6 address records can exceed the old UDP size limit. RFC 3226 requires affected DNS software to support EDNS0 so it can receive larger replies.

questions: what is the minimum edns0 size for dnssec
why is dns limited to 512 bytes
subtitle: Larger DNS answers need EDNS0 support from software that handles DNSSEC or IPv6 A6 records.

tldr.problem: The traditional DNS limit for UDP messages is 512 octets. DNSSEC signatures and A6 records can make replies too large, causing truncation and a retry over TCP.
tldr.mechanism: Servers and resolvers that support DNSSEC or A6 MUST support EDNS0, advertise the required message size, and handle fragmented IPv4 and IPv6 UDP packets.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3226 updates RFC 2535 and RFC 2874. The unit metadata says RFCs 4033, 4034, and 4035 update RFC 3226.

today: RFC 3226 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2535 and RFC 2874. It has been updated by RFC 4033, RFC 4034, and RFC 4035.

sections.title: The 512-Octet Limit
sections.content:
RFC 1035 limits DNS messages sent over UDP to a 512-octet data payload. A larger answer may be truncated, leaving the requester to retry over TCP.

The RFC explains that TCP adds connection setup and teardown work and requires server connection state. A requester and server can avoid that fallback when they can exchange a larger UDP response.
sections.plainLanguage: The old UDP limit can cut a DNS reply short. The requester may then have to ask again using TCP, which adds extra steps.

sections.title: Why Some DNS Replies Are Larger
sections.content:
DNSSEC adds public-key signatures to resource-record sets. The RFC reports signature sizes from about 80 to 800 octets, with most between 80 and 200. TSIG adds at least 70 octets, and A6 answers may require several records to describe an address.

Large replies can also affect root and top-level domain name server records. EDNS0 lets a client advertise the largest UDP message it is willing to handle.
sections.plainLanguage: Signatures and multi-part address records add information to DNS replies. EDNS0 lets a client tell the server how large a UDP reply it can receive.

sections.title: Larger UDP Replies and Fragmentation
sections.content:
The RFC requires implementations that support DNSSEC or A6 to use messages larger than 512 octets. Larger UDP messages may be fragmented, so losing one fragment can make the answer unusable.

The document says modern operating systems handle fragmentation, while packet loss remains a concern. On links with high loss, TCP is more reliable; on links with low loss, one larger UDP exchange can avoid the extra TCP setup.
sections.plainLanguage: A large UDP reply may arrive in pieces, and losing one piece means the answer must be tried again. The RFC weighs that risk against the extra exchanges TCP requires.

sections.title: EDNS0 Size and Fragment Requirements
sections.content:
Software compliant with RFC 2535 MUST support EDNS0 and advertise at least 1220 octets; it SHOULD advertise 4000. Software compliant with RFC 2874 MUST advertise at least 1024 octets and SHOULD advertise 2048.

All entities compliant with either RFC MUST handle fragmented IPv4 and IPv6 UDP packets. A host supporting both RFCs MUST advertise the larger required value. For IPv6, the RFC recommends 1024-octet datagrams unless the path MTU is known.
sections.plainLanguage: DNSSEC support requires a larger advertised message size than A6 support. Software that supports both must advertise the larger requirement and handle fragmented UDP packets.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content: RFC 3226 says it adds no security considerations beyond those in RFC 2671, which defines EDNS0. Its IANA Considerations section says there are no actions for IANA.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC adds no new security rules beyond EDNS0 and requests no IANA actions.
